ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there is a blue pendulum bob/block, labeled with a mass of 2.0 kg, connected to the end of a black light string. The string length is labeled as 5.0 m by a gray double arrow along the direction of the string. The upper end of the string is at the suspension point in the upper right, next to a vertical dashed line/vertical reference line; the angle between the inclined string and the vertical direction is labeled as 53°. The position of the pendulum bob at the lowest point is also drawn at the vertically downward position. Reasoning: The pendulum bob is released from rest at the 53° position, and the light string does no non-conservative work, so mechanical energy is conserved. The vertical drop height from the initial position to the lowest point is h = L(1 - cos 53°). Substituting L = 5.0 m, h = 5.0(1 - cos 53°). From gravitational potential energy transforming into kinetic energy: mgh = (1/2)mv^2, the mass m cancels, v = sqrt(2gL(1 - cos 53°)). Taking g = 9.8 m/s^2, v = sqrt(2(9.8)(5.0)(1 - cos 53°)) ≈ sqrt(39.0) ≈ 6.25 m/s, about 6.3 m/s.

Compute the vertical drop from the initial position to the bottom as h = L(1 - cos 53°). Then set mgh = (1/2)mv^2, cancel m, and solve v = sqrt(2gL(1 - cos 53°)), giving about 6.3 m/s.

method.method_draft: Use tangential dynamics integrated along the arc. First read the diagram: the bob moves from an initial angular displacement of 53° from the vertical down to the vertical bottom position on a 5.0 m cord. From the text, take that the bob is released from rest and the cord is light, so tension does no tangential work. At an intermediate angle phi from the vertical, the tangential component of gravity is mg sin phi, so the tangential acceleration is a_t = g sin phi. Use the kinematic relation along the arc, v dv/ds = a_t, with ds = -L dphi as the angle decreases from 53° to 0°. Integrate from v = 0 at phi = 53° to v at phi = 0: ∫ v dv = gL ∫_0^{53°} sin phi dphi, giving v^2/2 = gL(1 - cos 53°), so v ≈ 6.3 m/s.
